title: Promises to Keep: How Jackie Robinson Changed America
author: Sharon Robinson
source: Promises to Keep: How Jackie Robinson Changed America (Scholastic Press, 2004)
citation: Robinson, Sharon. Promises to Keep: How Jackie Robinson Changed America. Scholastic Press, 2004.

sections.heading: A Daughter's Memoir of Courage

epigraph.quote: A life is not important except in the impact it has on other lives.

paragraphs: Written by his daughter, Sharon Robinson, Promises to Keep provides an intimate, photographically rich biography of Jack Roosevelt Robinson. Born into a Georgia sharecropper family in 1919 and raised in Pasadena, California, by a resilient single mother, Jackie was an extraordinary four-sport athlete at UCLA, excelling in football, basketball, track, and baseball.

However, in 1940s America, racial segregation was codified into law and culture. Major League Baseball had maintained a strict, unwritten 'color line' for over six decades, barring African American athletes from big league diamonds and confining them to the Negro Leagues. Jackie knew the sting of Jim Crow segregation intimately: denied hotel rooms, forced to eat on team buses, and court-martialed in the U.S. Army for refusing to move to the back of a segregated military bus.

sections.heading: Branch Rickey's Noble Experiment and April 15, 1947

epigraph.quote: I want a ballplayer with guts enough not to fight back.

paragraphs: In 1945, Brooklyn Dodgers general manager Branch Rickey decided the time had come to integrate Major League Baseball. But Rickey knew that baseball ability was only half the battle. In a historic three-hour meeting, Rickey shouted simulated racial slurs in Jackie's face, demanding: 'I need a player who can take the insults, the beanballs, the spiked cleats, and have guts enough not to fight back.' Jackie accepted the challenge, understanding that his conduct would open or close doors for millions of Black Americans.

On April 15, 1947, Jackie Robinson took the field at Ebbets Field wearing Brooklyn Dodgers number 42, breaking the color barrier. Despite death threats, hostile opposing teams, and vitriolic taunts from stands, Jackie maintained disciplined silence, letting his electric base running, defensive brilliance, and clutch hitting speak for him. Winning Rookie of the Year in 1947 and Most Valuable Player in 1949, Jackie Robinson did more than integrate baseball; he ignited the modern American Civil Rights movement, demonstrating that excellence, dignity, and courage can dismantle prejudice.
